cards.key: He has 2 valence electrons, but it sits in group 18 (8A).

cards.p: On the left and in the middle are the metals (shiny, conductive), at the upper right the nonmetals, between them the metalloids, and at the far right the noble gases. Metallic character increases to the left and down.

etk.soru: Put each element in the right group.
ogeler: It sits on the left of the table in 1A, but it is a nonmetal.

cards.p: The main group number gives the number of valence electrons, with He as the only exception. Group 1A is called the alkali metals, 2A the alkaline earth metals, 7A the halogens and 8A the noble gases.

once.soru: Chlorine is in group 7A. How many electrons are in its outer shell?

secenekler.neden: The main group number gives the number of valence electrons. An element in group 7A has 7 valence electrons.
Elements in group 1A have 1 valence electron.
17 is chlorine's total number of electrons. Its outer shell has 7.

cards.p: Going down a group, the number of shells increases, so the atom gets bigger. Going right across a period, the number of protons increases, the nucleus pulls the electrons harder, and the atom gets smaller. A cation is smaller than its atom, and an anion is bigger.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><defs><marker id='periyodik-tablo-6' viewBox='0 0 10 10' refX='9' refY='5' markerWidth='6' markerHeight='6' orient='auto'><path d='M0 0L10 5L0 10z' fill='var(--acc)'/></marker></defs><g font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--ink)'><text x='40' y='28'>Li</text><text x='80' y='28'>Be</text><text x='120' y='28'>B</text><text x='160' y='28'>C</text><text x='200' y='28'>N</text><text x='240' y='28'>O</text><text x='280' y='28'>F</text></g><g fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.4' stroke='var(--c1)'><circle cx='40' cy='50' r='16'/><circle cx='80' cy='50' r='13'/><circle cx='120' cy='50' r='11'/><circle cx='160' cy='50' r='10'/><circle cx='200' cy='50' r='9'/><circle cx='240' cy='50' r='8'/><circle cx='280' cy='50' r='7'/><circle cx='40' cy='103' r='20'/><circle cx='40' cy='160' r='26'/></g><text x='68' y='107' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)'>Na</text><text x='72' y='164' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)'>K</text><line x1='100' y1='82' x2='290' y2='82' stroke='var(--acc)' stroke-width='2' fill='none' marker-end='url(#periyodik-tablo-6)'/><text x='195' y='102' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--ink)'>right across a period: smaller</text><line x1='100' y1='118' x2='100' y2='182' stroke='var(--acc)' stroke-width='2' fill='none' marker-end='url(#periyodik-tablo-6)'/><text x='110' y='155' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)'>down a group: bigger</text></svg>
cards.key: It increases down a group and decreases to the right. A cation is smaller than its atom, and an anion is bigger than its atom.

cards.p: Ionization energy increases to the right across a period and decreases down a group. There are two exceptions. Going from Be to B and from N to O, the ionization energy drops, because the s² and half-full p³ configurations are more stable.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><defs><marker id='periyodik-tablo-7' viewBox='0 0 10 10' refX='9' refY='5' markerWidth='6' markerHeight='6' orient='auto'><path d='M0 0L10 5L0 10z' fill='var(--ink)'/></marker></defs><line x1='40' y1='170' x2='310' y2='170' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='1.5' fill='none' marker-end='url(#periyodik-tablo-7)'/><line x1='40' y1='170' x2='40' y2='22' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='1.5' fill='none' marker-end='url(#periyodik-tablo-7)'/><line x1='36' y1='30' x2='44' y2='30' stroke='var(--ink)' fill='none'/><text x='34' y='34' font-size='12' text-anchor='end' fill='var(--ink)'>25</text><text x='34' y='174' font-size='12' text-anchor='end' fill='var(--ink)'>0</text><polyline points='40,94 54,32 67,140 81,118 95,124 108,107 122,89 136,94 149,73 163,49 177,141 191,127 204,136 218,124 232,111 245,112 259,97 273,82 286,146 300,136' fill='none' stroke='var(--acc)' stroke-width='2.5'/><g fill='var(--c5)'><circle cx='54' cy='32' r='4'/><circle cx='163' cy='49' r='4'/><circle cx='273' cy='82' r='4'/></g><g fill='var(--c4)'><circle cx='67' cy='140' r='4'/><circle cx='177' cy='141' r='4'/><circle cx='286' cy='146' r='4'/></g><g font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)'><text x='62' y='34'>He</text><text x='170' y='48'>Ne</text><text x='280' y='80'>Ar</text><text x='60' y='160'>Li</text><text x='170' y='160'>Na</text><text x='280' y='164'>K</text></g><text x='48' y='18' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)'>Ionization energy (eV)</text><text x='305' y='190' font-size='12' text-anchor='end' fill='var(--ink)'>Atomic number (1-20)</text></svg>
cards.key: Group 2A has a higher ionization energy than 3A, and 5A higher than 6A. This is because the s² and p³ configurations are spherically symmetric and more stable.

cards.p: As electrons are removed one by one, each one takes more energy. When the valence electrons run out and an inner shell is reached, the energy jumps suddenly. The number of electrons before the jump gives the group number.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><text x='160' y='18' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700' fill='var(--ink)'>Mg (2-8-2): successive ionization energies</text><line x1='40' y1='170' x2='290' y2='170' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='1.5'/><rect x='60' y='161.6' width='36' height='8.4' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.55'/><text x='78' y='156' font-size='11' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--ink)'>738</text><text x='78' y='186' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--ink)'>IE<tspan font-size='9' dy='3'>1</tspan></text><rect x='120' y='153.5' width='36' height='16.5' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.55'/><text x='138' y='147' font-size='11' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--ink)'>1451</text><text x='138' y='186' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--ink)'>IE<tspan font-size='9' dy='3'>2</tspan></text><rect x='180' y='82.0' width='36' height='88.0' fill='var(--c2)' fill-opacity='0.55'/><text x='198' y='76' font-size='11' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--ink)'>7733</text><text x='198' y='186' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--ink)'>IE<tspan font-size='9' dy='3'>3</tspan></text><rect x='240' y='50.0' width='36' height='120.0' fill='var(--c2)' fill-opacity='0.55'/><text x='258' y='44' font-size='11' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--ink)'>10543</text><text x='258' y='186' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--ink)'>IE<tspan font-size='9' dy='3'>4</tspan></text><text x='40' y='42' font-size='11' fill='var(--c2)'>IE₂ → IE₃: jumps more than 5 times</text><text x='40' y='58' font-size='12' font-weight='700' fill='var(--acc)'>→ 2 valence e⁻: group 2A</text><text x='300' y='198' font-size='10' text-anchor='end' fill='var(--muted)'>kJ/mol</text></svg>
cards.key: The number of electrons before the big jump equals the number of valence electrons and the main group number.

once.soru: An atom's successive ionization energies are 738, 1451 and 7733 kJ/mol. How many valence electrons does it have?

secenekler.neden: The first two electrons come off the outer shell easily. The third comes from an inner shell, so the energy jumps. This element, with 2 valence electrons, is magnesium in group 2A.
The third electron comes from an inner shell. So it is not a valence electron.
The second electron also comes off easily. The big jump comes after it.

cards.p: Electronegativity is how strongly an atom pulls the shared electrons in a bond toward itself. It increases to the right and decreases going down. Fluorine is the most electronegative, and oxygen is second.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><text x='160' y='20' font-size='13' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--ink)'>Electronegativity (Pauling), period 2</text><line x1='10' y1='160' x2='310' y2='160' stroke='var(--line)' fill='none'/><g fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.6'><rect x='18' y='131' width='24' height='29'/><rect x='58' y='113' width='24' height='47'/><rect x='98' y='99' width='24' height='61'/><rect x='138' y='83' width='24' height='77'/><rect x='178' y='69' width='24' height='91'/><rect x='218' y='57' width='24' height='103'/></g><rect x='258' y='41' width='24' height='119' fill='var(--c2)' fill-opacity='0.7'/><g font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--ink)'><text x='30' y='127'>1.0</text><text x='70' y='109'>1.6</text><text x='110' y='95'>2.0</text><text x='150' y='79'>2.6</text><text x='190' y='65'>3.0</text><text x='230' y='53'>3.4</text><text x='270' y='37'>4.0</text><text x='30' y='176'>Li</text><text x='70' y='176'>Be</text><text x='110' y='176'>B</text><text x='150' y='176'>C</text><text x='190' y='176'>N</text><text x='230' y='176'>O</text><text x='270' y='176'>F</text></g><text x='160' y='195' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--muted)'>Down the group: F 4.0 · Cl 3.2 · Br 3.0 · I 2.7</text></svg>
cards.key: Electronegativity increases to the right and up. Fluorine has the highest electronegativity.

once.soru: In the H–F bond, which atom are the shared electrons closer to?

secenekler.neden: Fluorine is the most electronegative element, and it pulls the electrons in the bond toward itself.
Hydrogen pulls much more weakly than fluorine.
Equal sharing happens only between two identical atoms, as in H–H.

cards.p: The energy released when a gaseous atom gains an electron is its electron affinity. The highest values are found in the halogens. Nonmetallic character increases to the right and up.

once.soru: Atoms of which group are most eager to gain electrons?

secenekler.neden: When halogens gain one electron, they reach a noble gas configuration. So their electron affinities are the highest.
These are eager to give up electrons, not to gain them.
Noble gases already have a stable configuration. So they are not eager to gain electrons.

cards.h: s, p, d and f blocks
cards.p: The subshell that the last electron enters sets the element's block. 1A, 2A and He are in the s block, and groups 3A–8A are in the p block. The B groups form the d block, and they are called transition metals. The lanthanides and actinides are in the f block.
cards.key: The main groups (A groups) are made of the s and p blocks. The transition metals (B groups) are in the d block.

once.soru: Iron (Fe) is in the B groups in the middle of the table. Which subshell does its last electron enter?

secenekler.neden: Fe is [Ar] 4s² 3d⁶, and the last electron enters 3d. The B groups in the middle of the table are the d block.
Elements ending in s are the two groups at the far left of the table.
Elements ending in p are the six groups on the right of the table.

cards.p:
• The modern table is arranged by atomic number and has 7 periods and 18 groups.
• The period number gives the number of shells, and the main group number gives the number of valence electrons.
• Metals are on the left, nonmetals at the upper right and noble gases at the far right.
• Toward the upper right, the radius decreases, and ionization energy and electronegativity usually increase.

quiz.q: Order these from highest to lowest electronegativity. (F: period 2, 7A; Cl: period 3, 7A; S: period 3, 6A; Na: period 3, 1A)
quiz.e: Electronegativity increases to the right and up. F is at the upper right (4.0). Cl is below it (3.2), S is to the left of Cl (2.6), and Na is at the far left of the period (0.9).

quiz.q: Order these isoelectronic ions from largest to smallest radius. (Z: S 16, Cl 17, K 19, Ca 20)
quiz.e: All four particles have 18 electrons. As the number of protons grows, the nucleus pulls the same electrons harder. So S²⁻ with 16 protons is the largest, and Ca²⁺ with 20 protons is the smallest.

quiz.q: A main-group atom has these successive ionization energies (kJ/mol): IE₁ = 578, IE₂ = 1817, IE₃ = 2745, IE₄ = 11 577. How many valence electrons does it have?
quiz.e: The big jump comes from IE₃ to IE₄ (2745 → 11 577). So the first 3 electrons are valence electrons, and the fourth comes from an inner shell. The atom is in group 3A, and it is aluminum.

quiz.q: Which one has the greatest metallic character? (Na: period 3, 1A; K: period 4, 1A; Mg: period 3, 2A; Al: period 3, 3A)
quiz.e: Metallic character increases to the left and down. K is both at the far left (1A) and below Na. Its valence electron is farthest from the nucleus, so it comes off most easily.
y: Na is also in group 1A, but K is below it. Going down, the electron comes off more easily.
Mg is to the right of Na. Metallic character decreases to the right.
Al is the farthest right of these three in period 3. So its metallic character is the smallest.

kimyasal-baglar.title: Interactions between chemical species
kimyasal-baglar.summary: The forces that hold atoms, ions and molecules together.

cards.p: A particle that carries chemical properties is called a chemical species. A chemical species can be an atom (He), an ion (Na+) or a molecule (H₂O). These species attract each other. So how tightly do they hold on?

once.soru: What kind of chemical species is Na⁺?

secenekler.neden: It is a charged sodium particle that has given up one electron.
The neutral atom is Na. The + charge shows that the atom has lost an electron.
A molecule forms when several atoms bond together.

cards.p: Attractions that take more than 40 kJ/mol to break are counted as strong (ionic, covalent, metallic), and those that take less are weak (van der Waals, hydrogen bonds).

once.soru: Which one is a strong interaction?

secenekler.neden: This bond holds atoms together inside a molecule, and breaking it takes a lot of energy.
This interaction is between molecules and counts as weak.
It is a weak attraction between molecules.

cards.p: Noble gases have a full outer shell, so they hardly react. Other atoms tend to complete their outer shell to 8 electrons, which is called an octet. H and Li complete it to 2 electrons, which is called a duet.

once.soru: Neon hardly ever reacts. Why?

secenekler.neden: Neon has 8 electrons in its outer shell. It has no electrons to gain or give up.
It is the outer-shell electrons that decide reactions.
Neon has 10 electrons.

cards.h: Ionic bonds and the ionic lattice
cards.p: A metal gives up electrons and becomes a cation, and a nonmetal gains electrons and becomes an anion. Oppositely charged ions attract each other, and this is called an ionic bond. There are no molecules in NaCl. The ions form a lattice.

cards.h: Formulas and names of ionic compounds
cards.p: In the formula of an ionic compound the charges add up to zero. For example, in Al₂O₃, 2·(+3) + 3·(−2) = 0. A compound is named by saying the cation first and then the anion. NaCl is sodium chloride, and Fe₂O₃ is iron(III) oxide.

cards.key: Single-atom anions end in -ide. Cl⁻ is chloride, O²⁻ oxide, S²⁻ sulfide, F⁻ fluoride and N³⁻ nitride. For metals whose charge can vary, the charge is written as a Roman numeral.

cards.p: In some ions, several atoms carry the charge together. OH⁻ is hydroxide, NO₃⁻ nitrate, SO₄²⁻ sulfate, CO₃²⁻ carbonate and NH₄⁺ ammonium. If more than one of these ions is needed, it goes in parentheses, as in Ca(OH)₂.

once.soru: What is the formula of the compound made of Ca²⁺ and OH⁻ ions?

secenekler.neden: Two OH⁻ are needed to balance the +2 charge. The polyatomic ion goes in parentheses.
Without parentheses the 2 multiplies only H, and there are not two O atoms.
The charges add up to +1, not zero.

cards.p: Nonmetals share their electrons, and both nuclei pull on the shared electron pair. This is called a covalent bond. H₂ has one shared pair, O₂ has two and N₂ has three.

cards.p: In compounds of two nonmetals, the numbers of atoms are given by prefixes: mono, di, tri, tetra, penta and hexa. Mono is not used for the first element. For example, CO is carbon monoxide, and N₂O₅ is dinitrogen pentoxide.

once.soru: What is the name of CO₂?

secenekler.neden: There is one C (mono is not used) and two O (di). So the name is carbon dioxide.
Mono is not used for the first element.
In a compound of two nonmetals, the number of O atoms is given by a prefix.

cards.p: The shared pair shifts toward the more electronegative atom. So the H–Cl bond is polar, and the H–H bond is nonpolar. In symmetrical CO₂ the bond dipoles cancel out. Bent H₂O is a polar molecule.

cards.h: Metallic bonds: a sea of electrons
cards.p: Metal atoms let go of their valence electrons, and these electrons move freely through the metal. The attraction between the cations and this sea of electrons is called a metallic bond. That is why metals conduct and can be hammered into shape.

once.soru: At room temperature Cl₂ is a gas and I₂ is a solid. Why do I₂ molecules hold on more tightly?

secenekler.neden: In a big molecule the electrons shift more easily. So the London forces get stronger.
I₂, made of two identical atoms, is nonpolar.

secenekler.yazi: There are ionic bonds between them
secenekler.neden: There are only weak attractions between I₂ molecules.

cards.p: An ion–dipole attraction happens between an ion and a polar molecule. When salt dissolves in water, Na+ pulls on water's δ− oxygen, and Cl− pulls on its δ+ hydrogens.

once.soru: When salt dissolves in water, which end of the water molecule does the Na⁺ ion attract?

secenekler.neden: The oxygen end of water has a partial negative (δ−) charge and attracts the positive ion.
The hydrogen end of water is δ+ and repels the Na⁺ ion.
Water is polar, so its ends have different charges.

cards.p: The attraction you just saw is formed only by H bonded to F, O or N. H₂O, NH₃ and HF have hydrogen bonds. CH₄ and H₂S do not.

cards.p: During boiling, only the attractions between molecules break. In electrolysis, which splits a substance with electricity, the O–H bonds break and H₂ and O₂ form. What decides the type of change is not the strength of the bond but whether a new substance forms.

etk.soru: Wrap up the topic: match each example with the interaction that holds its particles together.

cards.p:
• Chemical species are atoms, ions and molecules.
• Ionic bonds form by electron transfer, covalent bonds by sharing, and metallic bonds in a sea of electrons.
• In an ionic compound the charges add up to zero. Covalent compounds are named with prefixes.
• Van der Waals forces and hydrogen bonds are weak interactions.
• The test for a chemical change is that a new substance forms.

quiz.q: Sort each substance by the type of bond that holds its atoms together.
quiz.e: In NaCl and KCl, the metal gives up electrons and the nonmetal gains them, forming ionic bonds. In H<sub>2</sub>, HCl and N<sub>2</sub>, nonmetals share electrons, forming covalent bonds. In Cu and Fe, cations sit in a sea of electrons, forming metallic bonds.

quiz.q: Match each event with the interaction that explains it.
ciftler: Oxygen dissolving a little in water
quiz.e: When salt dissolves, the ions attract the oppositely charged ends of water, which is an ion–dipole interaction. Polar water creates a temporary dipole in nonpolar O<sub>2</sub>. Water's high boiling point comes from hydrogen bonds. The attraction between nonpolar molecules comes from momentary dipoles (London).

quiz.q: Match each formula with its systematic name.
quiz.e: In an ionic compound, the cation is read first and then the anion. In FeO iron has a +2 charge, so (II) is written in its name. In N₂O₄, made of two nonmetals, the numbers of atoms are given by prefixes.

quiz.q: Which molecule has polar bonds but is itself nonpolar?
quiz.e: The C=O bonds are polar, but in linear O=C=O the two bond dipoles point in opposite directions and are equal, so they cancel out.
y: H₂O is a bent molecule. Its bond dipoles do not cancel, so the molecule is polar.
HCl has only one bond, so there is no other bond to cancel its dipole. So the molecule is polar.
The Cl–Cl bond is between identical atoms, so the bond itself is nonpolar.

maddenin-halleri.title: States of matter
maddenin-halleri.summary: Learn the solid, liquid, gas and plasma states, changes of state and the phase diagram.

cards.h: Kinetic theory and the three states
cards.p: By kinetic theory, particles are always moving, and they speed up as the temperature rises. The state of a substance is set by a contest between the attraction among particles and their motion. In a solid, attraction wins. In a gas, motion wins.

once.soru: What happens to water molecules when you heat the water in a container?

secenekler.neden: Temperature is a measure of the particles' average energy of motion.
The size of the molecules does not change. What changes is their speed and the distance between them.
Particles never stop. They speed up when heated.

cards.p: In crystalline solids the particles form an ordered lattice, and the substance melts sharply at a definite temperature. Salt and ice are examples. In amorphous solids there is no order, and the substance softens slowly as it is heated. Glass and plastic are examples.

cards.p: The force that holds a crystal together decides its properties. Ionic crystals (NaCl) are hard and brittle. Covalent network crystals (diamond) are very hard to melt. Molecular crystals (ice) melt easily. Metallic crystals (Cu) conduct.

etk.soru: Match each solid with its type of crystal.

cards.key: When a molecular solid melts, the weak interactions between molecules break, not the covalent bonds.

once.soru: Why does diamond melt only at a very high temperature?

secenekler.yazi: It is a covalent network crystal
secenekler.neden: A whole diamond is one covalent network. To melt it, strong bonds must break.
Diamond has no separate molecules.
Diamond is made only of carbon atoms and contains no ions.

cards.p: Liquids flow because their particles slide past each other. The resistance to flow is called viscosity. Liquids with strong attractions have high viscosity, which is why honey flows more slowly than water. Viscosity drops as a liquid warms up.

cards.key: If you heat a liquid, its viscosity drops. Warm honey flows more easily.

cards.p: A molecule at the surface is pulled only sideways and inward. So the surface behaves like a stretched skin, and this is called surface tension. Water has high surface tension because of hydrogen bonds. Soap and heat lower surface tension.

cards.key: Drops take a round shape, because surface tension makes the surface as small as possible.

once.soru: How does a water strider walk on water without sinking?

secenekler.neden: The water surface acts like a stretched skin and holds up the light insect.
The insect does not sink into the water. The water surface holds it up.
Viscosity is resistance to flow. It does not explain being held up at the surface.

cards.p: In a closed container, once the rates of evaporation and condensation are equal, the pressure of the vapor is called the equilibrium vapor pressure. Vapor pressure rises with temperature. Liquids with weak attractions between particles, such as acetone, have high vapor pressure.

cards.p: When the vapor pressure equals the outside pressure, bubbles form inside the liquid, and this is called boiling. Evaporation happens at any temperature and only at the surface. If the outside pressure drops, the boiling point drops too.
cards.key: On a mountain, water boils below 100 °C. In a pressure cooker it boils at about 120 °C, which is why food cooks quickly there.

cards.p: The ratio of the vapor pressure in the air to the saturated vapor pressure is called relative humidity. At 100% relative humidity the air is saturated. When humidity is high, sweat evaporates poorly and the air feels hotter.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><rect x='50' y='30' width='44' height='120' fill='none' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='1.5' stroke-dasharray='4 3'/><rect x='50' y='90' width='44' height='60' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.45'/><line x1='40' y1='150' x2='104' y2='150' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='72' y='84' font-size='13' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700' fill='var(--c1)'>50%</text><text x='112' y='40' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)'>saturated vapor pressure</text><text x='112' y='56' font-size='12' font-weight='700' fill='var(--ink)'>23.8 mmHg (25 °C)</text><text x='112' y='104' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)'>water vapor in the air</text><text x='112' y='120' font-size='12' font-weight='700' fill='var(--c1)'>11.9 mmHg</text><text x='160' y='174' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700' fill='var(--acc)'>relative humidity = 11.9 / 23.8 × 100 = 50%</text><text x='160' y='193' font-size='11' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--muted)'>High humidity, sweat evaporates poorly: the air feels hotter</text></svg>
cards.key: The temperature your body senses is called the feels-like temperature. Relative humidity is the vapor pressure divided by the saturated vapor pressure, times 100.

once.soru: At the same 32 °C, why does a humid coastal city feel hotter than a dry desert city?

secenekler.neden: The air is close to full of vapor. So sweat cannot evaporate and cool the body.
The temperature is the same in both cities. The difference is the humidity.
What makes the felt difference is sweating, which depends on humidity.

cards.p: In a very hot gas, or one in a strong electric field, atoms lose electrons. This ionized gas, made of electrons and positive ions, is called plasma. The Sun, lightning and neon lights are examples of plasma.

once.soru: Which one is in the plasma state?

secenekler.neden: In lightning the air gets so hot that atoms lose electrons and an ionized gas forms.
Water vapor is an ordinary gas, and its molecules are not ionized.
Dry ice is solid CO₂.

cards.p: A substance above its critical temperature cannot be liquefied even by compression, and it is called a gas. A substance below its critical temperature is called a vapor, and it liquefies under pressure. That is why propane can be kept as a liquid in a tank.

once.soru: At room temperature, oxygen will not liquefy no matter how much you compress it. Why?

secenekler.yazi: It is above its critical temperature
secenekler.neden: Oxygen's critical temperature is about −119 °C. At room temperature, pressure alone is not enough.
Size does not decide liquefaction. The temperature relative to the critical value does.
Above the critical temperature, no amount of pressure causes liquefaction.

cards.h: Changes of state and the heating curve
cards.p: Melting, evaporation and sublimation absorb heat, so they are endothermic changes. Their reverses release heat, so they are exothermic changes. On the flat parts of the heating curve, the heat added goes into overcoming attraction, and the temperature stays constant.

etk.soru: Tap the numbers on water's phase diagram.

noktalar.acik: At low temperature and high pressure, water is ice.
Between the melting and vaporization curves, water is liquid.
At high temperature and low pressure, water is a gas (vapor).
At the triple point, solid, liquid and gas are in equilibrium together. For water this point is 0.01 °C and about 0.006 atm.
The liquid–gas curve ends here. Above this temperature, water vapor cannot be liquefied by pressure.

cards.key: On the curves, two states are in equilibrium. Water is an exception, because ice melts when pressure rises. CO₂'s triple point is at 5.1 atm, so dry ice sublimes at 1 atm.

cards.p:
• The state of a substance is set by the attraction between particles and their energy of motion.
• Crystalline solids melt sharply, and amorphous solids melt by softening.
• A liquid boils when its vapor pressure equals the outside pressure.
• Below the critical temperature there is vapor, above it gas. Plasma is ionized gas.
• For a change of state use Q = m·L, and for heating use Q = m·c·ΔT.

quiz.q: 20 g of ice at 0 °C melts and warms to water at 20 °C. How many calories of heat does it absorb in total? (Heat of fusion L = 80 cal/g, specific heat of water c = 1 cal/g·°C)
quiz.e: Melting (the flat part) takes Q = m·L = 20·80 = 1600 cal. Warming (the sloped part) takes Q = m·c·ΔT = 20·1·20 = 400 cal. The total is 2000 cal.

quiz.q: Water is boiled in an open pot at the places below. Order the boiling temperatures from lowest to highest.
quiz.e: Water boils when its vapor pressure equals the outside pressure. Higher up, air pressure drops and the boiling point falls. In a pressure cooker the pressure is above 1 atm.

quiz.q: Match each event with the fact that explains it.
ciftler: Dry ice turning into gas at 1 atm without melting
Ice melting below 0 °C under high pressure
Ice is less dense than water
Propane staying liquid in a tank
Pasta cooking slowly on a mountain
quiz.e: 1 atm is below CO₂'s triple point, so liquid CO₂ cannot form. Ice is less dense than water, so pressure makes melting easier. Propane is below its critical temperature, so it liquefies under pressure. On a mountain, water boils at a lower temperature.

quiz.q: The critical temperatures of some gases are given. Which one can be liquefied at 25 °C just by raising the pressure?
quiz.e: A substance liquefies under pressure only while it is below its critical temperature. 25 °C is below the critical temperature of NH₃ only. So at room temperature NH₃ is a vapor.
y: 25 °C is above CH₄'s critical temperature. CH₄ must first be cooled below −82 °C.
Helium's critical temperature is −268 °C. At 25 °C no pressure can liquefy it.
At 25 °C, H₂ is far above its critical temperature. Pressure alone is not enough.

temel-kanunlar.title: The basic laws of chemistry
temel-kanunlar.summary: Mass is conserved and ratios are fixed. Learn the basic laws that describe chemistry with numbers.

cards.p: Lavoisier weighed reactions in closed containers. He found that the total mass of the reactants equals the total mass of the products. Atoms are not destroyed or created from nothing. They are only rearranged.

once.soru: A reaction takes place in a closed container. What does the balance show when it is over?

secenekler.neden: While the container is closed, no atom escapes or is added. So mass is conserved.
Gas cannot escape from a closed container.
No matter enters a closed container from outside.

cards.h: Why does mass change in an open container?
cards.p: When wood burns in the open, the ash left behind is lighter, because CO<sub>2</sub> and water vapor escape into the air. When magnesium burns, the product gets heavier, because oxygen from the air joins it. In both cases conservation still holds.

cards.h: Calculation: which substance is left over?
cards.p: Say 3 g of hydrogen reacts with 40 g of oxygen. The ratio is 1:8, so the hydrogen combines with only 24 g of oxygen. That leaves 16 g of oxygen, and 27 g of water forms.

cards.key: Divide each mass by its ratio number. The substance that gives the smaller result is used up completely.

cards.p: Two elements can form more than one compound. According to Dalton, when the mass of one element is held fixed, the masses of the other give a ratio of small whole numbers. For example, CO has 16 g of oxygen and CO2 has 32 g.

once.soru: Between N₂O and NO₂, what is the ratio of oxygen masses for equal nitrogen?

secenekler.neden: If you equalize nitrogen, the compounds become N₂O and N₂O₄. The ratio of oxygen atoms is 1 : 4.
You must first make the numbers of nitrogen atoms equal.
N₂O has less oxygen.

cards.h: When is there no multiple proportion?
cards.p: A multiple proportion is looked for only between different compounds of the same two elements. For compounds with the same empirical formula, such as N2O4 and NO2, the ratio comes out 1:1, and this does not count as a multiple proportion.

once.soru: Between which pair is there a multiple proportion?

secenekler.neden: These are two separate compounds that the same two elements form in different ratios.
They have the same empirical formula (NO₂), and the ratio comes out 1:1.

secenekler.yazi: 5 g of water and 50 g of water
secenekler.neden: These are the same compound, so there is no multiple proportion to look for.

once.soru: At the same temperature and pressure, which has more molecules: 1 L of hydrogen or 1 L of oxygen?

secenekler.neden: Under the same conditions, equal volumes of gases contain equal numbers of particles.
A heavier molecule does not change the number.
A lighter molecule does not change the number.

cards.p: Dalton explained these laws with his atomic theory. In his view, elements are made of atoms, atoms combine in small whole-number ratios, and they are not destroyed in a reaction. The idea that atoms cannot be divided no longer holds today.

cards.key: You saw in the topic on atomic models that atoms can be divided and that isotopes exist. But the idea that atoms are conserved in reactions still holds today.

once.soru: Which part of Dalton's atomic theory no longer holds today?

secenekler.neden: We know that atoms are made of protons, neutrons and electrons.
This idea still holds today, and conservation of mass rests on it.
This idea still holds today, and formulas rest on it.

cards.p:
• In a closed container the total mass is conserved.
• In a compound the mass ratio is fixed. In water H:O is 1:8.
• By the law of multiple proportions, when the shared element is held fixed, the masses of the other are in small whole-number ratios.
• At the same temperature and pressure, gas volumes combine in whole-number ratios.
• Atoms can be divided, and isotopes exist.

quiz.q: Nitrogen and oxygen form two different compounds. For 7 g of nitrogen, 4 g of oxygen bonds in the first compound and 16 g in the second. How many times the oxygen mass in the first is the oxygen mass in the second?
quiz.e: Nitrogen is fixed at 7 g in both compounds. The oxygen masses are 4 : 16, or 1 : 4. This is the law of multiple proportions, and the compounds are N₂O and NO₂.

quiz.q: Sort each pair by whether a multiple proportion can be looked for between them.
quiz.e: A multiple proportion is looked for between compounds of the same two elements with different empirical formulas. H<sub>2</sub>O and H<sub>2</sub>S do not share two elements, NO<sub>2</sub> and N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> have the same empirical formula, and 5 g and 50 g of water are the same compound.

quiz.q: In water, 1 g of hydrogen always combines with 8 g of oxygen. 12 g of hydrogen and 64 g of oxygen react to form water. When the reaction is complete, how many grams of water have formed?
quiz.e: 64 g of oxygen combines with 64 ÷ 8 = 8 g of hydrogen. 8 + 64 = 72 g of water forms, and 12 − 8 = 4 g of hydrogen is left over.

quiz.q: At the same temperature and pressure, 2 L of H₂ and 1 L of O₂ react completely to form water vapor. Which is true?
o: The total gas volume stays 3 L
quiz.e: The volumes are in a 2:1:2 ratio, and 3 L of gas turns into 2 L of water vapor. Volume is not conserved, but mass always is.
y: Gas volumes do not simply add up. By the ratio 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, 3 L of gas turns into 2 L of vapor.
Volume can go down, but mass is conserved in every reaction. Atoms do not disappear.
Volumes follow the mole ratio. By the equation 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, 2 L of H₂ forms 2 L of vapor.

tepkimeler.title: Chemical reactions and equations
tepkimeler.summary: Learn about reactions, writing and balancing equations, what is conserved and the types of reactions.

once.soru: Which one is a chemical reaction?

secenekler.neden: Iron and oxygen form a new substance, iron oxide.
Melted ice is still water. This is a change of state.
When the water evaporates, the sugar is left behind. This is a physical change.

cards.p: In a reaction, bonds break, atoms rearrange and new bonds form. Atoms are not destroyed or created from nothing. In a physical change the substance keeps its identity. For example, melted ice is still water.

cards.p: In an equation, the reactants are written to the left of the arrow and the products to the right. The number in front of a formula is the coefficient. The state of a substance is shown as (s) solid, (l) liquid, (g) gas or (aq) dissolved in water.

once.soru: In the equation 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, which side is water on?

secenekler.neden: The substances to the right of the arrow are products, and they form in the reaction.
The reactants are to the left of the arrow, and they are H₂ and O₂.
Water is written only to the right of the arrow, as a product.

cards.p: When balancing, you change only the coefficients. The subscripts decide what the substance is. If you change H2O to H2O2, you have turned water into hydrogen peroxide.

cards.p: The goal of balancing is to have the same number of each atom on both sides. Count the atoms and start with the most complex compound. Leave single elements such as O<sub>2</sub> and H<sub>2</sub> for last. If you get a fraction, multiply all the coefficients.

once.soru: When balancing C₂H₆ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O, what do you adjust first?

secenekler.neden: First balance the atoms in compounds. Leave O₂, a single element, for last.
O₂ is a single element. If you leave it for last, it is easy to adjust.
Subscripts are never changed. Only coefficients are.

cards.p: In the equation Fe + O<sub>2</sub> → Fe<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>, oxygen comes in twos on the left and threes on the right, and the common multiple is 6. First write 3O<sub>2</sub> and 2Fe<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>, then add 4Fe on the left.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><text x='16' y='26' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='start'>Start</text><text x='195' y='26' font-size='14' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>Fe + O₂ → Fe₂O₃</text><text x='195' y='44' font-size='11' fill='var(--c2)' text-anchor='middle'>O: 2 on the left, 3 on the right</text><line x1='12' y1='58' x2='308' y2='58' stroke='var(--line)'/><text x='16' y='82' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='start'>Balance O</text><text x='195' y='82' font-size='14' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>Fe + 3O₂ → 2Fe₂O₃</text><text x='195' y='100' font-size='11' fill='var(--c1)' text-anchor='middle'>common multiple of 2 and 3 is 6: 6 O = 6 O</text><line x1='12' y1='114' x2='308' y2='114' stroke='var(--line)'/><text x='16' y='138' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='start'>Balance Fe</text><text x='195' y='138' font-size='15' fill='var(--c3)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>4Fe + 3O₂ → 2Fe₂O₃</text><text x='195' y='158' font-size='11' fill='var(--c1)' text-anchor='middle'>2 × 2 = 4 Fe on the right → 4Fe on the left</text><text x='160' y='186' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>Check: 4 Fe = 4 Fe, 6 O = 6 O</text></svg>
cards.key: The result is 4Fe + 3O₂ → 2Fe₂O₃. The (III) in the compound's name shows that iron has a +3 charge.

once.soru: In the equation 4Fe + 3O₂ → 2Fe₂O₃, how many oxygen atoms are on the right?

secenekler.neden: 2 × 3 = 6. The 3O₂ on the left also contains 6 O atoms.
Coefficient 2, subscript 3: multiply them.
The coefficient and the subscript are not added. They are multiplied.

cards.h: What is conserved in a reaction?
cards.p: In a reaction the nuclei do not change. Only electrons are rearranged. So the kinds and numbers of atoms, the mass and the charge are conserved. The number of molecules and the volume may not be.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><rect x='10' y='12' width='145' height='136' rx='6' fill='var(--c3)' fill-opacity='0.08' stroke='var(--c3)'/><rect x='165' y='12' width='145' height='136' rx='6' fill='var(--c2)' fill-opacity='0.08' stroke='var(--c2)'/><text x='82' y='34' font-size='13' fill='var(--c3)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>Conserved</text><text x='237' y='34' font-size='13' fill='var(--c2)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>Can change</text><text x='82' y='62' font-size='11' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>kinds and numbers of atoms</text><text x='82' y='84' font-size='11' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>total mass</text><text x='82' y='106' font-size='11' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>total charge</text><text x='82' y='128' font-size='11' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>total number of electrons</text><text x='237' y='62' font-size='11' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>number of molecules</text><text x='237' y='84' font-size='11' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>volume (for gases)</text><text x='237' y='106' font-size='11' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>physical state</text><text x='237' y='128' font-size='11' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>color, properties</text><text x='160' y='172' font-size='14' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃</text><text x='160' y='192' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>4 molecules → 2 molecules, but 2 N and 6 H on both sides</text></svg>
cards.key: In an ionic equation the charges must also balance. For example, in Zn + 2H⁺ → Zn²⁺ + H₂ the total charge on both sides is +2.

once.soru: In the reaction N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃, what is not conserved?

secenekler.neden: 4 molecules go in, and 2 molecules come out.
Mass is conserved in every reaction.
There are 2 N and 6 H on both sides.

cards.p: Combustion is a substance reacting with oxygen and releasing heat. With enough oxygen, CO<sub>2</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>O form. As you just saw, with too little oxygen, CO and soot form too.

cards.key: Combustion needs fuel, oxygen and an ignition temperature. If any one is removed, burning stops. N₂ combines with oxygen by absorbing heat, so it is counted as not burning.

cards.p: In a synthesis reaction, two or more substances combine to form a single product. If 1 mol of a compound forms from its elements, it is called a formation reaction. In a decomposition reaction, a compound breaks down into simpler substances.

cards.p: As you just saw, when two ionic solutions mix, some ions form a solid that does not dissolve. This solid is called a precipitate. Spectator ions are left out of the equation, as in Ag+ + Cl− → AgCl(s).
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><text x='160' y='20' font-size='11' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>AgNO₃(aq) + NaCl(aq) → AgCl(s) + NaNO₃(aq)</text><rect x='31' y='58' width='118' height='81' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.12'/><rect x='31' y='124' width='118' height='15' fill='var(--muted)' fill-opacity='0.45'/><path d='M30 40 V140 H150 V40' fill='none' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='52' y='84' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>Na⁺</text><text x='112' y='80' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>NO₃⁻</text><text x='78' y='104' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>NO₃⁻</text><text x='128' y='106' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>Na⁺</text><text x='90' y='158' font-size='11' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>AgCl(s) settles to the bottom</text><text x='236' y='52' font-size='12' fill='var(--c3)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>Net ionic equation</text><text x='236' y='74' font-size='13' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>Ag⁺ + Cl⁻ → AgCl(s)</text><text x='236' y='110' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>Spectator ions</text><text x='236' y='130' font-size='13' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>Na⁺ and NO₃⁻</text><text x='236' y='148' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>stay unchanged</text><text x='160' y='188' font-size='11' fill='var(--acc)' text-anchor='middle'>In the net equation, atoms and charge must balance too.</text></svg>
cards.key: The spectator ions here are Na⁺ and NO₃⁻. Salts of Na⁺, K⁺, NH₄⁺ and NO₃⁻ dissolve in water. AgCl, BaSO₄ and CaCO₃ dissolve only slightly.

cards.p: In an acid-base reaction, the H+ ion of the acid and the OH− ion of the base combine to form water. Usually a salt and water are produced. In redox reactions, electrons are exchanged.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><rect x='10' y='10' width='300' height='84' rx='6' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.08' stroke='var(--c1)'/><rect x='10' y='104' width='300' height='88' rx='6' fill='var(--c5)' fill-opacity='0.08' stroke='var(--c5)'/><text x='22' y='30' font-size='12' fill='var(--c1)' text-anchor='start' font-weight='700'>Acid-base (neutralization)</text><text x='160' y='54' font-size='11' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>HCl(aq) + NaOH(aq) → NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l)</text><text x='160' y='78' font-size='13' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>net: H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O</text><text x='22' y='124' font-size='12' fill='var(--c5)' text-anchor='start' font-weight='700'>Redox (electron exchange)</text><text x='160' y='148' font-size='13' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>2Mg(s) + O₂(g) → 2MgO(s)</text><text x='160' y='168' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>Mg gives up electrons, O gains electrons.</text><text x='160' y='184' font-size='11' fill='var(--c5)' text-anchor='middle'>One reaction: combustion + synthesis + redox</text></svg>
cards.key: Both are covered in detail in their own topics. A reaction can belong to more than one type.

once.soru: What type of reaction is HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O?

secenekler.neden: An acid and a base combine to form a salt and water. This is called neutralization.
In decomposition a single compound breaks down. Here two substances react.
Combustion happens with oxygen.

cards.p:
• In a reaction bonds break and form again, and a new substance forms.
• When balancing, only coefficients change, not subscripts.
• Atoms, mass and charge are conserved. The number of molecules can change.
• Combustion needs fuel, oxygen and an ignition temperature. Incomplete combustion forms CO.
• The types of reactions are combustion, synthesis, decomposition, acid-base, precipitation and redox.

quiz.q: When C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub> + a O<sub>2</sub> → b CO<sub>2</sub> + c H<sub>2</sub>O is balanced with the smallest whole numbers, what is a?
quiz.e: For C atoms b = 3, and for H atoms c = 4. There are 3·2 + 4 = 10 O atoms on the right. So a = 5.

quiz.q: In a chemical reaction in a closed container, which of these are conserved? Put each one in the right group.
quiz.e: In a reaction the nuclei do not change, and atoms are only rearranged. So the kinds and numbers of atoms, the mass and the charge are conserved. The number of molecules and the volume can change. For example, in N<sub>2</sub> + 3H<sub>2</sub> → 2NH<sub>3</sub>, 4 molecules form 2 molecules.

quiz.q: Match each reaction with its type.
quiz.e: Methane burns with oxygen. Nitrogen and hydrogen combine into a single product, so this is synthesis. The electrolysis of water is a compound breaking down, which is decomposition. Ag<sup>+</sup> and Cl<sup>−</sup> form a precipitate. HCl and NaOH give a salt and water, which is an acid-base reaction.

quiz.q: When BaCl₂ and Na₂SO₄ solutions are mixed, a white precipitate forms. What is the net ionic equation?
quiz.e: BaSO₄ dissolves only slightly in water, so it precipitates. Na⁺ and Cl⁻ are spectator ions that stay unchanged on both sides, and they are not written in the net equation.
y: Na⁺ salts dissolve in water. Na⁺ and Cl⁻ are spectator ions and do not form a precipitate.
This is the full equation. In the net equation the spectator ions are removed.
Na⁺ salts dissolve in water, so Na₂SO₄ does not precipitate.

mol.title: The mole and chemical calculations
mol.summary: Learn the mole, Avogadro's number, finding formulas, stoichiometry and yield.

etk.soru: n = m / M and N = n · N<sub>A</sub>. Change the mass and the molar mass. (Water: M = 18 g/mol)

cards.key: The molar mass of water is 18 g/mol, and 0.5 mol of water contains 3.01×10²³ molecules. Whatever unit you start from and wherever you go, convert to moles first.

once.soru: How many moles is 36 g of water (M = 18 g/mol)?

secenekler.neden: The division is upside down. You need 36 / 18, not 18 / 36.
You divide the mass by the molar mass, you don't multiply.

cards.p: At the same temperature and pressure, equal numbers of moles of gas take up equal volumes. At STP (0 °C, 1 atm), 1 mole of gas takes up 22.4 L, and at room conditions about 24.5 L.

cards.key: 22.4 L/mol applies only to gases at STP. Under other conditions, use PV = nRT from the Gases topic.

cards.p: The mass percent of an element is its mass in the formula divided by the molar mass, times 100. In NaCl (M = 58.5), Na is 39.3% and Cl is 60.7%. These percentages do not depend on the sample size.

cards.key: The mass of Na is 23 and that of Cl is 35.5. The percentages stay constant because of the law of definite proportions.

once.soru: What is the mass percent of hydrogen in water (H₂O, M = 18)? (H = 1)

secenekler.neden: 67% is the ratio of atom counts (2 of 3 atoms). It is not the mass ratio.
Hydrogen atoms are very light, so they add little to the mass.

cards.p: The smallest whole-number ratio of atoms is called the empirical formula. To find it, turn the percentages into grams in a 100 g sample and divide by the molar masses. Then divide all mole numbers by the smallest one.

once.soru: A compound has 2 mol of H for every 1 mol of C. Which is its empirical formula?

secenekler.neden: The smallest whole-number ratio is 1 : 2.
The ratio is written backwards.
This could be a molecular formula. The simplest ratio is CH₂.

cards.p: The molecular formula is a whole-number multiple of the empirical formula, written as (CH₂O)n. CH₂O has a molar mass of 30 g/mol. If the compound is 180 g/mol, then n = 6 and the formula is C₆H₁₂O₆ (glucose).

once.soru: A compound with empirical formula CH has a molar mass of 78 g/mol. What is its molecular formula? (CH = 13)

secenekler.neden: 78 / 13 = 6. So the formula is (CH)₆, that is C₆H₆, and the compound is benzene.
CH has a mass of 13. To reach 78 you need 6 times that.
C₂H₂ has a molar mass of 26 g/mol, not 78.

cards.p: The coefficients in an equation give the mole ratio, not the mass ratio. In N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃, 1 mol of N₂ combines with 3 mol of H₂ to give 2 mol of NH₃.

once.soru: In 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, how many moles of O₂ react with 4 mol of H₂?

secenekler.neden: The coefficient ratio is H₂ : O₂ = 2 : 1. So 4 mol of H₂ needs 2 mol of O₂.
The mole ratio is 2 : 1, not 1 : 1.
The coefficient of O₂ is half that of H₂.

cards.p: First convert the given substance to moles. Then use the coefficients to find the moles of the substance you want, and switch to the unit you need. For example, in CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O, 8 g of CH₄ gives 22 g of CO₂.

cards.p: The largest amount of product calculated from the limiting reactant is called the theoretical yield. Because of losses, you actually get less. The percent yield is the actual yield divided by the theoretical yield, times 100.

cards.key: Yield cannot exceed 100%. If it does, the product is most likely wet or impure.

once.soru: In theory 36 g of water should form, but 27 g was obtained. What is the percent yield?

secenekler.neden: The actual yield cannot be larger than the theoretical yield. The ratio is upside down.
25% is the part that was lost, not the yield.

cards.p: Give each component of a mixture an unknown and set up two equations. One equation is for the total amount, the other for the product.

cards.key: If 0.5 mol of a CH₄–C₂H₆ mixture at STP burns to give 0.7 mol of CO₂, then x + y = 0.5 and x + 2y = 0.7. This gives 0.3 mol of CH₄ and 0.2 mol of C₂H₆.

once.soru: Each C atom gives one CO₂ when it burns. How many moles of CO₂ form when 1 mol of C₂H₆ burns?

secenekler.neden: C₂H₆ has 2 C atoms, and each one forms a CO₂.
There are two carbon atoms in one molecule.
6 is the number of hydrogens.

cards.p:
• 1 mole is 6.02×1023 particles.
• Use n = m/M = N/NA. For gases at STP, n = V/22.4.
• Percentages give the empirical formula, and the molar mass gives the molecular formula.
• Coefficients give the mole ratio, so convert to moles first.
• The reactant that runs out decides the product. Yield is the actual amount divided by the theoretical amount.

quiz.q: How many grams is the CO<sub>2</sub> gas that takes up 4.48 L at STP? (C = 12, O = 16)
quiz.e: n = 4.48 / 22.4 = 0.2 mol. The molar mass of CO<sub>2</sub> is 44 g/mol, so m = 0.2 × 44 = 8.8 g.

quiz.q: Match each amount to its number of moles. (H = 1, C = 12, O = 16)
A compound is 80% C and 20% H by mass, and its molar mass is 30 g/mol. How many H atoms are in its molecular formula? (H = 1, C = 12)
quiz.e: 100 g contains 80 / 12 = 6.67 mol of C and 20 / 1 = 20 mol of H. The ratio is 1 : 3, so the empirical formula is CH<sub>3</sub> (15 g/mol). n = 30 / 15 = 2, and the molecular formula is C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub>. So the molecule has 6 H.

quiz.q: For the reaction N<sub>2</sub> + 3H<sub>2</sub> → 2NH<sub>3</sub>, a container holds 2 mol of N<sub>2</sub> and 3 mol of H<sub>2</sub>. When the reaction goes to completion, what is in the container?
quiz.e: 3 mol of H<sub>2</sub> reacts with only 1 mol of N<sub>2</sub>. The H<sub>2</sub> runs out, 2 mol of NH<sub>3</sub> forms and 1 mol of N<sub>2</sub> is left over.
y: 3 mol of H<sub>2</sub> uses up only 1 mol of N<sub>2</sub>. The leftover 1 mol of N<sub>2</sub> stays in the container.
The limiting reactant is H<sub>2</sub>. 2 mol of N<sub>2</sub> would need 6 mol of H<sub>2</sub>, but there are only 3 mol.
4 mol of NH<sub>3</sub> would need 6 mol of H<sub>2</sub>. 3 mol of H<sub>2</sub> gives at most 2 mol of NH<sub>3</sub>.

gazlar.title: Gases
gazlar.summary: Learn the relationships between pressure, volume, temperature and moles, the gas laws and real gases.

cards.p: Gases compress easily, fill their container and mix in any proportion. Four quantities describe a gas: pressure P, volume V, temperature T and number of moles n. Temperature is always used in kelvins.

cards.key: The kelvin temperature is the Celsius temperature plus 273. 0 °C is not zero, it is 273 K. Gases have low densities.

once.soru: In gas calculations, how many kelvins is 27 °C?

secenekler.neden: The gas laws work with kelvins. You add 273 to the Celsius value.
You add 273, you don't subtract it.

cards.p: 1 atm equals 760 mmHg and about 101.3 kPa. A manometer measures gas pressure. If the mercury is lower on the gas side, then Pgas = P0 + h.

once.soru: In an open-end manometer, the mercury is 10 cm lower on the gas side. The outside pressure is 76 cmHg. What is the gas pressure in cmHg?

secenekler.neden: The gas pushes the mercury harder than the outside air. So it is 76 + 10 = 86.
The mercury is lower on the gas side, so the gas is pushing harder.
That would be true for a closed-end manometer.

cards.p: At constant temperature and moles, pressure and volume are inversely proportional, and P₁·V₁ = P₂·V₂. If the volume is halved, the pressure doubles.

once.soru: Under the same conditions, which has more molecules: 1 L of H₂ or 1 L of O₂?

secenekler.neden: Under the same conditions, equal volumes of gases contain equal numbers of particles.
O₂ is heavier, but the number of particles is the same.
H₂ is lighter, but the number of particles is the same.

cards.p: If the moles are constant, the three laws combine into P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂. You cancel whatever quantity doesn't change from both sides. Temperature must be in kelvins.

once.soru: Both the pressure and the kelvin temperature of a gas double. What happens to its volume?

secenekler.neden: Doubling the pressure halves the volume, and doubling the temperature doubles it. The two effects cancel.
Raising the pressure shrinks the volume. The two effects work in opposite directions.
Raising the temperature also grows the volume, and the two effects cancel.

cards.h: The ideal gas law: PV = nRT
cards.p: P·V = n·R·T links all four quantities. If P is in atm, V in liters and T in kelvins, then R = 0.082 L·atm/(mol·K). In SI units, R = 8.314 J/(mol·K).

etk.soru: P·V = n·R·T, R = 0.082 L·atm/(mol·K). Change the moles, the temperature and the volume.

cards.key: For example, 0.5 mol of gas in a 4.1 L container at 27 °C has a pressure of P = 0.5·0.082·300 / 4.1 = 3 atm. If pressure is in kPa, use R = 8.314 L·kPa/(mol·K).

cards.p: If you substitute n = m/M, you get d = P·M/(R·T). Gas density increases with pressure and molar mass and decreases with temperature.

cards.key: Using density, the molar mass of an unknown gas is found from M = d·R·T/P.

once.soru: Why does a hot air balloon rise?

secenekler.neden: Heated air has a lower density. The cooler air around it pushes it up.
Hot air has mass too. There is just less of it in the same volume.
The flame heats the air. What lifts the balloon is the difference in density.

cards.p: According to kinetic theory, ideal gas particles move randomly, their volume is negligible and they don't attract each other. The average kinetic energy is directly proportional to absolute temperature.

cards.p: Real gas particles have volume and attract each other. So real gases deviate from ideal behavior at high pressure and low temperature. A gas above its critical temperature won't liquefy even when compressed.

cards.key: A gas below its critical temperature is called a vapor, and a vapor liquefies when compressed. The most nearly ideal gases are small, nonpolar ones such as He and H₂.

once.soru: Under which conditions does a gas behave most like an ideal gas?

secenekler.neden: Under these conditions the particles are far apart and fast. So their volume and attraction become negligible.
Under these conditions the particles are crowded and attraction matters.
At high pressure the particles' own volume becomes important.

cards.p:
• Temperature is always in kelvins, and 1 atm is 760 mmHg.
• The gas laws combine into P·V = n·R·T.
• Density is d = P·M/(R·T). By Graham's law, r ∝ 1/√M.
• Average kinetic energy depends only on temperature.
• Total pressure is the sum of the partial pressures. Real gases deviate at high pressure and low temperature.

quiz.q: A closed 8.2 L container holds 0.5 mol of ideal gas at 127 °C. What is the gas pressure in atm? (R = 0.082 L·atm/(mol·K))
quiz.e: T = 127 + 273 = 400 K. P = n·R·T / V = 0.5·0.082·400 / 8.2 = 2 atm. If you forget to convert to kelvins, you get 0.64 atm.

quiz.q: Two containers are joined by a closed valve. The 2 L one holds He at 3 atm and the 4 L one holds Ne at 1.5 atm. If the valve is opened at constant temperature, what is the final pressure in atm?
quiz.e: Each gas spreads into the total 6 L. P(He) = 3·2/6 = 1 atm and P(Ne) = 1.5·4/6 = 1 atm. By Dalton's law, P(total) = 1 + 1 = 2 atm. In short, you can write P₁V₁ + P₂V₂ = P(final)·V(total).

quiz.q: At the same temperature, order these gases from fastest to slowest spreading. (g/mol: H₂ 2, He 4, CH₄ 16, O₂ 32, CO₂ 44)
quiz.e: By Graham's law, the rate is inversely proportional to √M, so the gas with the smaller molar mass is faster. The order is H₂ > He > CH₄ > O₂ > CO₂.

quiz.q: Hydrogen is collected over water at 27 °C. The water levels inside and outside are equal, and the outside pressure is 750 mmHg. If the vapor pressure of water at 27 °C is 27 mmHg, what is the partial pressure of H₂ in mmHg?
quiz.e: The total pressure in the container equals the outside pressure and is made up of the pressures of H₂ and water vapor. So the pressure of H₂ is 750 − 27 = 723 mmHg. Adding the water vapor pressure is a common mistake.
y: You subtract the water vapor pressure, you don't add it. The total pressure is the sum of the pressures of H₂ and water vapor.
750 mmHg is the total pressure. It includes 27 mmHg of water vapor pressure, so the pressure of H₂ is less.
27 mmHg is the partial pressure of the water vapor. The pressure of H₂ is the total minus this value.

asit-baz.title: Acids, bases and salts
asit-baz.summary: Learn the definitions of acids and bases, pH, Ka, neutralization, salts and titration.

cards.p: Acids taste sour. Solutions of bases taste bitter and feel slippery. Dyes that change color in acids and bases are called indicators. Litmus turns red in acid and blue in base.

cards.key: Lemons and vinegar contain acids. Acids release CO₂ from limestone (CaCO₃), and this is how descalers work. Never taste anything in the lab.

once.soru: You dip litmus paper into lemon juice. What color does it turn?

secenekler.neden: Lemon contains acid, and litmus turns red in acid.
Litmus turns blue in base. Lemon is acidic.
Litmus is an indicator, and its color changes in acid.

cards.p: According to Arrhenius, an acid is a substance that releases H+ in water. The H+ bonds to water and forms H₃O+. A base is a substance that releases OH− in water. NH₃ is a base because it forms OH− with water.

etk.soru: Sort each substance by how it behaves in water: does it release H⁺ or form OH⁻?
ogeler: This is acetic acid, found in vinegar. It releases H⁺ in water (weak acid).
It has no OH in its structure, but it reacts with water and forms OH⁻.

cards.key: H₃O⁺ is the hydronium ion. The Arrhenius definition holds only for aqueous solutions.

once.soru: Which ion does HCl release when it dissolves in water?

secenekler.neden: HCl splits into H⁺ and Cl⁻ ions in water. A substance that releases H⁺ in water is an acid.
HCl has no OH group. Substances that release OH⁻ are bases.
HCl splits almost completely into ions in water.

cards.p: According to Brønsted–Lowry, an acid is a proton (H+) donor and a base is a proton acceptor. An acid that gives away a proton leaves behind its conjugate base. For example, the conjugate base of CH₃COOH is CH₃COO−.

once.soru: What does water do in the reaction NH₃ + H₂O → NH₄⁺ + OH⁻?

secenekler.neden: Water gives an H⁺ to NH₃ and becomes OH⁻. Here it acts like an acid.
NH₃ is the one that accepts the proton and becomes NH₄⁺.
Water reacts, loses an H⁺ and becomes OH⁻.

once.soru: A little acid is added to pure water. What happens to [OH⁻]?

secenekler.neden: At 25 °C the product [H₃O⁺][OH⁻] is constant. So when H₃O⁺ goes up, OH⁻ goes down.
The acid adds H₃O⁺. The product stays constant, so OH⁻ cannot increase.
The product is constant. When one goes up, the other has to go down.

cards.h: pH, pOH and the pH scale

once.soru: Ka values: 7×10⁻⁴ for HF and 1.8×10⁻⁵ for CH₃COOH. Which is the stronger acid?

secenekler.neden: The acid with the larger Ka ionizes more. HF has the larger Ka.
This acid has the smaller Ka and ionizes less.
The Ka values differ. The one with the larger Ka is stronger.

cards.p: For a strong monoprotic acid, [H₃O⁺] equals the acid concentration. For example, 0.01 M HCl has a pH of 2. For weak acids, use [H₃O⁺] ≈ √(Ka·C).

once.soru: What is the pH of a 0.001 M HCl solution?

secenekler.neden: HCl ionizes completely. [H₃O⁺] = 10⁻³ M, so pH = 3.
That is the concentration. pH is the negative logarithm of the concentration.
11 is the pOH. The pH of an acid is below 7.

cards.p: When an acid reacts with a base, a salt and water form. The real event is H₃O⁺ and OH⁻ joining to make water, and heat is released. Stomach remedies called antacids work this way.

cards.key: Antacids contain Mg(OH)₂ or NaHCO₃. Neutralization does not always give pH 7. The result depends on the salt that forms.

cards.p: H₂SO₄ can release two H⁺ and H₃PO₄ three. Ca(OH)₂ also releases two OH⁻. For complete neutralization, n(H⁺) = n(OH⁻).

cards.key: For example, 100 mL of 0.1 M H₂SO₄ releases 0.02 mol of H⁺. 100 mL of 0.2 M NaOH neutralizes it. CH₃COOH releases only one H⁺.

once.soru: How many moles of NaOH are needed to fully neutralize 0.1 mol of H₂SO₄?

secenekler.neden: H₂SO₄ releases two H⁺. 0.2 mol of H⁺ needs 0.2 mol of OH⁻.
Each H₂SO₄ releases two H⁺, but each NaOH releases only one OH⁻.
The acid is diprotic. So you need more base, not less.

cards.p: The anion of a weak acid or the cation of a weak base reaches equilibrium with water, and this is called hydrolysis. So the pH of a salt depends on the strength of the acid and base that formed it.

cards.key: The salt takes on the character of whichever side is strong. NH₄Cl is acidic and CH₃COONa is basic. If both are weak, compare Ka and Kb.

cards.p: Neutralizing an acid of unknown concentration drop by drop with a base of known concentration is called titration. When the acid is used up exactly, the equivalence point is reached and the pH jumps sharply.
cards.key: For a weak acid, the total amount of acid still counts. In a strong acid–strong base titration, the pH at the equivalence point is 7. In a weak acid–strong base titration, it is above 7.

once.soru: How many mL of NaOH of the same concentration are needed to neutralize 25 mL of HCl?

secenekler.neden: If the concentrations are equal, equal volumes contain equal moles. So 25 mL is enough.
That adds twice as much base. The acid runs out halfway, and the rest of the base is left over.
That is half of what is needed. Half of the acid stays un-neutralized.

cards.p: A solution that contains a weak acid and its conjugate base (CH₃COOH / CH₃COONa) is a buffer. When a little acid or base is added, its pH changes very little.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><defs><marker id='asit-12' viewBox='0 0 10 10' refX='9' refY='5' markerWidth='6' markerHeight='6' orient='auto-start-reverse'><path d='M0 0 L10 5 L0 10 z' fill='var(--c2)'/></marker></defs><text x='160' y='22' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>Adding 0.01 mol HCl to 1 L of solution</text><rect x='10' y='34' width='140' height='80' rx='6' fill='var(--c2)' fill-opacity='0.07' stroke='var(--c2)'/><rect x='170' y='34' width='140' height='80' rx='6' fill='var(--c3)' fill-opacity='0.07' stroke='var(--c3)'/><text x='80' y='54' font-size='13' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>Pure water</text><text x='80' y='80' font-size='15' fill='var(--c2)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>pH 7 → 2</text><text x='80' y='102' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>large change</text><text x='240' y='54' font-size='13' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>Acetate buffer</text><text x='240' y='80' font-size='15' fill='var(--c3)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>pH 4.74 → 4.66</text><text x='240' y='102' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>very small change</text><text x='160' y='136' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>0.1 M CH₃COOH + 0.1 M CH₃COONa</text><text x='160' y='160' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>added H₃O⁺ + CH₃COO⁻ → CH₃COOH + H₂O</text><text x='160' y='182' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>added OH⁻ + CH₃COOH → CH₃COO⁻ + H₂O</text></svg>
cards.key: A weak base with its conjugate acid also makes a buffer. Blood is protected by the H₂CO₃ / HCO₃⁻ buffer. A buffer's capacity is limited.

cards.p: Active metals react with acids to form a salt and H₂. Cu, Ag and Au do not give H₂ with HCl. Amphoteric metals such as Al and Zn also release H₂ with strong bases.

cards.key: When diluting, always add acid to water, never water to acid. Cu and Ag react with HNO₃, but they release NO or NO₂, not H₂.

cards.p: Most nonmetal oxides are acidic (CO₂, SO₂). Oxides of active metals are basic (Na₂O, CaO). Al₂O₃ and ZnO are amphoteric, and CO, NO and N₂O are neutral oxides.

once.soru: What is the solution like when CO₂ dissolves in water?

secenekler.neden: CO₂ forms carbonic acid with water. That is where the slight sourness of soda comes from.
Basic solutions come from metal oxides. C is a nonmetal.
CO₂ reacts with water and forms an acid.

cards.p:
• An acid donates a proton and a base accepts one.
• At 25 °C, pH + pOH = 14, and pH 7 is neutral.
• Strong acids and bases ionize completely, weak ones only partly.
• In neutralization, n(H⁺) = n(OH⁻). The salt that forms is not always neutral.
• Active metals form a salt and H₂ with acids.

quiz.q: What is the pH of a 0.005 M Ca(OH)₂ solution at 25 °C? (Ca(OH)₂ ionizes completely.)
quiz.e: Each Ca(OH)₂ releases two OH<sup>−</sup>. So [OH<sup>−</sup>] = 2 × 0.005 = 0.01 M and pOH = 2. The pH is 14 − 2 = 12.

quiz.q: At 25 °C, a 0.01 M solution of the weak acid HA has K<sub>a</sub> = 1×10⁻⁶. What is the pH of the solution?
quiz.e: [H₃O⁺] ≈ √(K<sub>a</sub>·C) = √(10⁻⁶ × 10⁻²) = √(10⁻⁸) = 10⁻⁴ M, so pH = 4. HCl at the same concentration would have a pH of 2.

quiz.q: Match each oxide to its type.
quiz.e: CO₂ forms an acid with water, and CaO forms a base. ZnO reacts with both acids and bases. CO reacts with neither, so it is neutral.

quiz.q: A 0.1 M CH₃COOH solution is titrated with 0.1 M NaOH. Which is true for the solution at the equivalence point at 25 °C?
quiz.e: At equivalence the solution contains CH₃COONa. The anion of the weak acid reacts with water and releases OH<sup>−</sup>, so the solution is basic.
y: Equal moles of a weak acid and a strong base do not give a neutral solution. CH₃COO<sup>−</sup> reacts with water and produces OH<sup>−</sup>.
At the equivalence point all of the acid has reacted. The CH₃COO<sup>−</sup> left in solution makes it basic.
The pH reaches 14 only with 1 M OH<sup>−</sup>. Here there is only acetate, a weak base.

kimya-her-yerde.title: Chemistry everywhere
kimya-her-yerde.summary: Learn about cleaning products, polymers, medicines, food and farm chemistry.

once.soru: What is the chemical name of the soda used to make a cake rise?

secenekler.neden: Baking soda is NaHCO₃. When heated it releases CO₂ and makes the dough rise.
NaCl is table salt.
CaCO₃ is limestone.

cards.p: Soap is the sodium or potassium salt of a fatty acid. The tail of a soap molecule sinks into the grease, and the head faces the water. The sphere that forms this way is called a micelle. The micelle keeps dirt suspended in water.

etk.soru: Tap the parts of the soap molecule and the micelle.

noktalar.acik: The tail is a long hydrocarbon chain. It is nonpolar, so it loves grease, not water.
The head is the ionic −COO⁻ end. It interacts well with polar water molecules.
Nonpolar grease does not dissolve in water. The soap's tails sink into the grease.
Water molecules surround the heads on the micelle's surface. This keeps the dirt suspended in water.
A polar solvent. The micelles carrying dirt spread through the water and rinse away.

cards.key: The ionic head loves water (hydrophilic) and the hydrocarbon tail loves grease (hydrophobic). Soap is made from fat and NaOH (with glycerol as a byproduct).

cards.p: Hard water contains a lot of Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺. Soap forms an insoluble scum with these ions and lathers poorly. When hard water is heated, CaCO₃ settles out, and this is how limescale forms in a kettle.

cards.p: Detergents are synthetic cleaners made from petroleum, and their structure is similar to soap. They don't form scum with Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺, so they lather even in hard water.

cards.p: The number inside the triangle on a plastic shows its type. 1 is PET, 2 HDPE, 3 PVC, 5 PP and 6 PS. Plastics stay in nature for hundreds of years and break into microplastics.

once.soru: What happens to a plastic bottle thrown into the sea?

secenekler.neden: Plastic breaks down very slowly in nature. It crumbles into microplastics.

secenekler.yazi: It rots in a few months
secenekler.neden: Microorganisms can't break down most plastics.
Plastics are nonpolar, so they don't dissolve in water.

cards.p: The substance that makes a medicine work is called the active ingredient. Too small a dose does nothing, and too much is poisonous. Antibiotics act on bacteria, not on viruses.

once.soru: What happens if someone with the flu takes an antibiotic?

secenekler.neden: The flu is a viral disease, and antibiotics act only on bacteria. Unnecessary use leads to resistance.
Antibiotics don't kill viruses.
An antibiotic gives no immunity, because it is not a vaccine.

once.soru: How does salt in brine keep food from spoiling?

secenekler.neden: Concentrated salt draws water out of microorganisms by osmosis. So the microorganisms can't multiply.
Salt does not produce heat.
Oxygen speeds up spoilage, and salt does not add oxygen.

once.soru: Rain carries excess fertilizer from a field into a lake. What happens in the lake?

secenekler.neden: Fertilizer feeds the algae too. As the algae rot, the oxygen in the water drops and the fish die.
Fertilizer pollutes the water, and the excess nutrients upset the balance.
The oxygen drops, so the fish die.

cards.h: Check the pH when choosing a product
cards.p: Limescale is a basic deposit, and an acidic product (vinegar) dissolves it. Greasy dirt comes off with a basic product (soap, baking soda). Never put acid on marble or strong base on aluminum.

once.soru: Which removes limescale stains in the shower most easily?

secenekler.neden: Limescale is CaCO₃, and the acid in vinegar dissolves it.
Soap is basic. It removes greasy dirt, but it does not dissolve limescale.
Baking soda is basic too, and it does not dissolve limescale.

cards.p:
• Soap is a fatty acid salt, and it carries dirt into water by forming micelles.
• In hard water soap forms scum, but detergent lathers.
• Never mix bleach with acidic or ammonia cleaners.
• Plastic is a polymer and lasts a long time in nature.
• Watch the dose of medicines and read food labels.

quiz.q: Match each farm chemical to its job.
quiz.e: Insecticides, herbicides and fungicides are pesticides used against insects, weeds and fungi. Fertilizer doesn't kill pests. It gives plants nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium.

quiz.q: Sort each property under soap or detergent.
quiz.e: Soap is the Na or K salt of a fatty acid. It forms scum with Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ and breaks down more easily in nature. Detergent is a synthetic substance made from petroleum, and it lathers in hard water too. Detergents with added phosphate can cause algae growth in lakes.

quiz.q: A bag of chips says 0.8 g of salt per 100 g. If you eat the whole 30 g bag, how many grams of salt do you get?
quiz.e: The values on the label are per 100 g. So 0.8 × 30 / 100 = 0.24 g of salt.

quiz.q: Someone mixes bleach with an ammonia glass cleaner to clean the windows. What happens?
o: They neutralize to salt and water
quiz.e: Hypochlorite reacts with ammonia and forms chloramine gases that burn the airways. Never mix bleach with acid or with ammonia.
y: Mixing two cleaners doesn't clean better. Together these two produce a toxic gas.
Ammonia is a weak base and bleach is basic too. What happens here is not neutralization but chloramine formation.
NaOCl reacts with ammonia and releases toxic chloramine.
